facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The height of the pillar, from the top to the bottom of its base, is 7.21 m (23 ft 8 in), 1.12 m (3 ft 8 in) of which is below ground.
facts.text: The Iron Pillar of Delhi stands at a total height of 7.21 metres from its underground base to the tip of its bell capital, with about 1.12 metres resting below the modern stone floor.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The Delhi Iron Pillar is a large mass of iron, weighing about 6 tons, which is nearly the weight of a full-grown male elephant!
facts.text: Structural and computational analyses estimate the total weight of the forge-welded wrought iron pillar to be approximately 6.0 tonnes.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: having in faith fixed his mind upon (the god) Vishnu, this lofty standard of the divine Vishnu was set up on the hill (called) Vishnupada.
facts.text: The earliest Sanskrit inscription engraved on the pillar records that a monarch named Chandra erected it as a standard of Vishnu on the hill named Vishnupada.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Balasubramaniam demonstrates that the lack of rust is due to the formation of a protective layer of misawite (δ-FeOOH), as well as a layer of crystalline phosphates, catalyzed by the presence of comparatively high levels of phosphorus in the iron.
facts.text: In 2002, metallurgist R. Balasubramaniam of IIT Kanpur demonstrated that the pillar's rust resistance is due to a thin protective surface layer composed of misawite and iron hydrogen phosphate hydrate.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Moreover, the pillar iron contains a relatively larger weight fraction of P (average composition 0.25%) which will aid in inducing passivity in iron.
facts.text: Elemental assays by IIT Kanpur established that the pillar possesses an average phosphorus concentration of roughly 0.25 percent, compared to modern wrought iron which rarely exceeds 0.05 percent.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: In ancient India lime wasn't added in the processed of iron from blast furnaces. Lime is responsible for carrying away most of the phosphorus present, in the modern processes.
facts.text: Ancient Indian smelters produced this corrosion-resistant wrought iron by directly reducing iron ore with charcoal in open bloomery hearths without adding limestone flux, preserving phosphorus in the finished metal.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: Fleet (1898) identified this place with Mathura... Based on archaeological and astronomical evidence, Balasubramaniam (2000) and Meera Dass (2004) identified Vishnupadagiri with modern Udayagiri.
facts.source_name: IIT Kanpur & Archaeological Survey of India
facts.text: While epigraphist J. F. Fleet asserted that the original hill Vishnupadagiri was located in Mathura, researchers R. Balasubramaniam and Meera Dass argued it was modern Udayagiri near Vidisha based on astronomical alignments during summer solstices.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: The identity of king Chandra of the Delhi iron pillar Sanskrit inscription has been critically addressed.
facts.text: Scholars dispute whether King Chandra in the eulogy refers to Gupta Emperor Chandragupta II or to the 4th-century ruler King Chandravarman of Pushkarana in Rajasthan.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: Alexander Cunningham read the inscription as follows: 'Samvat Dihali 1109 Ang Pāl bahi'... Buddha Rashmi Mani (1997) read it as follows: Samvat Kinllī 1109 Angapala bādi.
facts.text: Historians debate the reading of a Samvat 1109 inscription carved on the shaft, with Alexander Cunningham reading it as Tomar King Anangpal peopling Delhi and B. R. Mani interpreting it as Anangpal tightening the iron pillar in 1052 CE.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: The Brahman also predicted that as long as the pillar stood, the dominion would remain with King Anang Pal's family. However, harboring doubts... foot of the pillar was found wet with the blood of Vasuki... This Dhili Killi (loose pillar), is said to be the origin of the name of the ancient city of Delhi.
facts.text: A popular oral legend claims King Anangpal uprooted the pillar because he doubted a priest's warning that it was anchored into the head of the cosmic serpent Vasuki, causing it to loosen forever and giving Delhi its name.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: There is a popular tradition that it was considered good luck if you could stand with your back to the pillar and make your hands meet behind it.
facts.text: A widespread local belief maintained that standing with one's back to the pillar and successfully wrapping one's arms around it brought good luck and answered prayers.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: A fence was erected around the pillar in 1997 in response to damage caused by visitors... it was found that this practice was harming the naturally occurring protective film on the pillar's surface.
facts.text: In 1997, the Archaeological Survey of India enclosed the pillar with an iron fence because constant human rubbing and sweat were eroding the protective misawite layer on its lower section.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: when, in battle in the Vanga countries (Bengal), he kneaded (and turned) back with (his) breast the enemies who, uniting together, came against (him); – he, by whom, having crossed in warfare the seven mouths of the (river) Sindhu, the Vahlikas were conquered.
facts.text: The Mehrauli pillar's poetic verse proclaims that King Chandra defeated a confederacy of enemies in Vanga and crossed the seven tributaries of the Indus to conquer the Vahlikas.
